The Blue swallow (Hirundo atrocaerulea) is a small aerial insectivore that inhabits montane grasslands and wetlands across eastern and southern Africa. Freshly laid eggs, incubated at a steady temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], typically hatch after fifteen days [ab = fifteen days], a development period that aligns closely with that of other Hirundo species given similar thermal regimes. The altricial nestlings emerge at a notably modest body mass, with the wet weight at birth averaging just 1.4 grams [Wwb = 1.4 grams]. This initial mass is considerably lower than the ultimate wet weight attained by adults, which reaches approximately 13.9 grams [Wwi = approximately 13.9 grams], reflecting a more than ninefold increase in body mass from hatching to maturity. Comparative data from the congeneric barn swallow suggest that these developmental timings are tightly coupled to metabolic constraints and ambient conditions during the breeding season.

Reproductive output in the Blue swallow is characterized by a moderate annual investment. Typical clutch size in this species is between two and three eggs per nesting attempt, and field records indicate that females regularly produce two such clutches each year. The maximum reproductive rate is thus realized when females lay approximately 2.6 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 2.6 eggs per clutch] and successfully complete two clutches annually [F_R_i = two clutches annually], resulting in a yearly production of over five eggs per breeding female. This pattern is consistent with that of many temperate and subtropical Hirundinidae, where extended parental care and the energetic demands of aerial foraging constrain clutch frequency. The incubation period and nestling development, unfolding under the elevated body temperatures typical of active passerines at approximately 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], also govern the subsequent milestones of juvenile growth and the timing of key life-history transitions.

Fledging represents a critical developmental threshold for young Blue swallows, marking the transition from complete dependency on parental provisioning to the initial stages of independent flight. Under the thermal conditions characteristic of active metabolic periods for this species, which hover near 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], nestlings achieve their first flight and depart the nest at just 22 days after hatching [tx = 22 days after hatching]. This relatively short nestling period is typical for members of the genus and reflects the high predation pressure that nests experience in open grassland habitats. The subsequent attainment of puberty occurs considerably later, as individuals require additional weeks to complete somatic growth and develop the flight musculature and foraging proficiency necessary for survival. Field data indicate that gonadal maturation is reached at 66 days after hatching [tp = 66 days after hatching], a duration that encompasses both the fledgling phase and a period of intensive post-fledging care during which juveniles continue to receive food from adults while refining their hunting skills at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C].

First reproduction in the Blue swallow is not attempted during the same calendar year as hatching, a pattern that distinguishes this species from some smaller, more r-selected congeners. The onset of the first successful breeding event typically occurs at 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching], meaning that most individuals do not breed until their second summer at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This deferred reproductive schedule, unfolding at the species' characteristic active body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], likely reflects the time required to secure a suitable nesting territory and to accumulate sufficient fat reserves to support the energetic demands of egg formation and incubation. Consequently, the reproductive lifespan of a typical adult is compressed into a limited number of breeding seasons. The initial wet weight of a newly hatched chick is just 1.67 grams [Ww0 = 1.67 grams], a value that represents the mass of the embryo at the moment of hatching, before any exogenous feeding has occurred.

Longevity data for the Blue swallow remain sparse, but studies on the closely related barn swallow (Hirundo rustica) provide a useful comparative benchmark. In the absence of species-specific demographic records spanning multiple decades, the maximum recorded lifespan in the wild for the Blue swallow is estimated at 16 years [am = 16 years] under the elevated core body temperatures averaging 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C] that characterize active passerine metabolism. This figure is derived from mark-recapture studies of the congeneric barn swallow, which exhibits similar body size, migratory tendencies, and life-history strategies. Such a lifespan, when combined with the deferred age at first reproduction of one year, implies that a female Blue swallow may participate in up to fifteen breeding seasons over her lifetime. The species' comparatively modest annual fecundity, with two clutches per year, is thus offset by an extended period of reproductive activity, allowing individuals to achieve a substantial net lifetime reproductive output.
